title: SRE GPU swap and capacity stretch checklist (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a practical, compact runbook for on-call SREs to follow when a GPU-backed node experiences hardware degradation or complete accelerator failure, and when immediate capacity pressure requires a short-term capacity stretch. It is intended as a prioritized checklist and step-by-step guide for safe node removal, temporary capacity injection, and controlled recovery.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to GPU worker nodes in the production inference cluster (k8s clusters: inference-prod-us-west, inference-prod-eu).
- Assumes standard node labeling (role=worker, accelerator=gpu) and that we have a hot-spare pool labeled gpu-spare=true in the cluster or in the dedicated capacity fleet.
- Assumes access to kubectl, terraform/infra-runbooks for cloud reprovisioning, and ability to schedule physical GPU swaps via colo on-call.
- This is a draft checklist; operational playbooks (acceptance tests, physical safety steps for colo techs) live in Confluence linked above.

When to use this checklist:
- Node shows repeated ECC errors, GPU timeouts, or driver crashes (dmesg + nvidia-smi errors).
- Pod eviction patterns show sustained OOMs or GPU device allocation failures tied to a node.
- Multiple nodes report degraded GPU health and immediate capacity shortfall threatens SLAs.

Quick triage (5–10m):
1) Confirm alert context: check alert details in PagerDuty, link to Grafana alert.
2) Identify affected node(s): kubectl get nodes -l accelerator=gpu -o wide and cross-check node hostname in alert.
3) Check GPU health directly: ssh node && sudo dmesg | tail -n 200; nvidia-smi -q; sudo journalctl -u nvidia-device-plugin -n 200
4) Verify running pods and critical customers: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide | grep <node>
5) If noisy/unrecoverable: proceed to cordon + drain.

Cordon and drain (preserve KV cache where possible):
- Rationale: best-effort to migrate traffic while minimizing token re-computation/KV cache loss. If the node hosts long-running KV-warmed GPUs (e.g., models with large KV cache), prefer graceful drain.

Commands (example):
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=120 --timeout=20m
Notes:
- For pods with local state (persistent volumes), coordinate with owning service owner before deletion.
- If drains hang due to custom preStop hooks, escalate to the service owner; consider --grace-period=0 as last resort.

If drain blocked by accelerated-device-plugin pods:
- restart device plugin: kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart daemonset/nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset
- If device plugin repeatedly fails, capture logs and skip pods controlled by the plugin (they will be re-bound).

Temporary capacity stretch (when cluster-level capacity SLOs are endangered):
Goal: restore capacity quickly while avoiding permanent cluster churn. Prefer soft, reversible steps first.
Options (in order):
1) Warm a spare node from gpu-spare pool (if present): label selection should auto-attach to the serving autoscaler.
2) Trigger a fast provisioning job (cloud): terraform apply with instance count +1 using the spare template (ops-infra runbook).
3) Enable canary low-latency burst instances: create new nodegroup with smaller batch-size overrides to reduce per-token latency impact.
4) Temporarily reduce model batch sizes and increase concurrency thresholds for non-critical routes via Redwood Console (route-level config) to spread requests across more GPUs.

Commands / tickets to trigger provisioning (examples):
- infra runbook: /ops/provision-gpu-spare (internal runbook)
- Terraform target: terraform apply -var 'asg_desired=+1' -target=module.gpu_autoscaling_group
- Slack: @infra on-call, message: "Requesting hot-provision of 1x a100 spare in us-west for capacity stretch — incident <PagerDuty-ID>"

Physical GPU replacement (if node hardware confirmed faulty):
1) Mark node as cordoned and note the time and pods migrated.
2) Create a replacement ticket for colo team with precise hostname, rack, and serial numbers (copy node-describe output). Include screenshots of nvidia-smi errors and dmesg snippets.
3) If swap requires FRU replacement: schedule a short maintenance window and update stakeholders.
4) Use spare node to absorb load while swap occurs. Do not re-introduce the repaired node until acceptance tests pass.

Re-provisioning / smoke tests before rejoin:
- After physical swap and BIOS/firmware checks, ensure node has: up-to-date OS image, matching kernel and container runtime, correct GPU driver version used in cluster.
- Acceptance checklist (run on node):
  - sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade (or cloud-image verification)
  - nvidia-smi -> report GPU presence and ECC status
  - run simple inference smoke test (curl to local model endpoint or run containerized test image)
  - run 10-minute load test using the standard bench harness: bench/inference-smoke --duration 600 --concurrency 4
  - kubectl label node <node> accelerator=gpu,role=worker and remove gpu-spare if applicable

Rejoin sequence:
- kubectl uncordon <node>
- Monitor pod scheduling and ensure kubelet attaches GPU devices for pods.

Post-incident verification (15–60m):
- Metrics to watch (Grafana dashboards):
  - GPU allocation failures per minute
  - Token latency p50/p95 for top 5 customer routes
  - Pod restart count and OOM events
  - Node ready status and kubelet errors
- Example PromQL snippets (paste into Grafana):
  - sum(rate(kube_pod_container_state_restarts_total[5m])) by (node)
  - sum(rate(node_gpu_ecc_errors_total[5m])) by (node)
  - sum(rate(redwood_api_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (route)

(continued)

Escalation and communication:
- If more than two nodes require replacement in the same AZ, escalate to SRE lead and infra manager immediately.
- Update the incident Slack channel with status checkpoints: Initial triage, cordon/drain start and end times, capacity stretch actions taken, physical swap ticket created, rejoin completed.
- Use template: "[INCIDENT <PagerDuty-ID>] Node <node> cordoned at <time>, drained X pods. Provisioned +1 spare in us-west. Swap ticket created TKT-1234."

Diagnostics collection (for engineering and postmortem):
- Save outputs to incident bucket: /sre/incidents/<incident-id>/node-<node>-diagnostics.txt
- Minimum artifacts: dmesg, nvidia-smi -q, kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet -n 500), pod logs for affected pods, prometheus snapshot link, node describe output.

Runbook caveats and lessons learned (notes to self):
- Draining long-warmed KV caches increases token cost for customers dramatically — prefer warm spares where feasible.
- In a capacity shortage, reducing batch size on a per-route basis can be less disruptive than spinning up cheaper-but-slower instances.
- We need a lightweight feature in Console to mark a node as GPU-hot-warm so that autoscaler avoids killing it during scale-in. Ticketed: JIRA-OPS-1487.

Open TODOs for this doc (work items):
- Add physical safety checklist for colo technicians (swap torque specs, ESD precautions). Owner: Michael Chen.
- Add a short script to snapshot warmed KV state where supported. Owner: Diego Morales.
- Validate terraform hot-provision runbook with infra on-call and add a pre-approved escalation step. Owner: Aisha Patel.

After-action:
- Create incident timeline in Confluence and link to JIRA ticket for root cause analysis.
- If regression observed in model outputs post-recovery, open a model-regression ticket and attach eval traces.

Appendix — useful commands/snippets (copy-paste):
- Identify pods on node: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- Cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- Drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=120 --timeout=20m
- Uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
- Device plugin restart: kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart daemonset/nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset
- Quick GPU health: ssh <node> -- nvidia-smi -q | egrep "Ecc Mode|Temperature|Compute Mode" -A2

Contact list:
- SRE on-call: see PagerDuty schedule
- Infra on-call: @infra-oncall (Slack)
- Colo hardware ops: colo-ops@redwood.com

Revision history:
- 2024-10-12: initial draft created by Aisha Patel
- 2024-11-02: expanded capacity-stretch section and added TODOs (collaborators: Diego, Lena)

End of doc.
